name: State
first: A value that SwiftUI keeps for a view while the view is on the screen, and that makes SwiftUI run the view's body again when it changes.

dependsOn.why: State belongs to a view, and a change to it makes SwiftUI run that view's body again.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `taps` is state of `Counter`, a view, and its `body` reads `taps`.

dependsOn.why: State is a property wrapper that SwiftUI provides, so a state property is a wrapped property.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `@State` before `taps` makes `taps` a wrapped property of the property wrapper `State`.

dependsOn.why: The example changes its state in the closure of a modifier that runs when the view appears.
dependsOn.whyInExample: `onAppear` is a modifier of the `Text`, and its closure adds 1 to `taps`.

dependsOn.why: The code that changes the state is a closure, which SwiftUI calls later.
dependsOn.whyInExample: The braces after `onAppear` hold a closure, which SwiftUI calls when the view appears.

what.is: State is a value that SwiftUI keeps for a view. A property marked `@State` keeps its value while SwiftUI makes the view's structure again and again. When code changes the value, SwiftUI runs the view's `body` again, so that what the view shows matches the new value.
what.afterExample: `Counter` keeps `taps` in state. When the view appears, line 9 adds 1 to `taps`, and SwiftUI runs `body` again, so line 6 prints the new value.
what.problem: SwiftUI can make a view's structure again whenever it needs it, so a plain stored property would start from its first value each time. The code in `body` cannot change a stored property either. State keeps a value while the view is on the screen, lets code change it, and shows each change.
what.how: SwiftUI keeps the value of a state property in storage of its own, outside the structure. Reading `taps` reads that storage. Writing `taps` changes the storage, and makes SwiftUI run `body` again.

when.text: Use state for a value that only this view and the views inside it use, such as how many times a button was tapped. Mark it `private`, because only the view itself sets it.
Don't use state for data that several screens share, or that must still be there after the app quits. A state property lasts only while its view is on the screen.

parts.name: The state property `taps`, line 4
parts.text: The attribute `@State` makes `taps` a wrapped property of `State`, the property wrapper that SwiftUI provides. Its first value is 0, and it is `private`, so only `Counter` reads and writes it. SwiftUI keeps its value, so each time `body` runs, `taps` reads the value that SwiftUI kept.

steps.text: Line 14 makes a `Counter`, and an `ImageRenderer` for it. An `ImageRenderer` draws a view into an image, as a window draws it on a screen, so this program can run SwiftUI without a window.
Line 15 asks the renderer for its image, so SwiftUI starts to draw `Counter`. It makes the storage for `taps`, with the value 0, and runs `body`.
The `Text` appears, so SwiftUI calls the closure of `onAppear`. Line 9 adds 1 to `taps`, and the storage that SwiftUI keeps now holds 1.
The state changed, so SwiftUI runs `body` again. Line 6 reads `taps`, which is now 1, and prints {{Taps: 1}}.

end.text: SwiftUI keeps the value of `taps`. The change on line 9 made SwiftUI run `body` again, with the new value.
